question: Under the federal fire extinguisher carriage table (33 CFR 175.320), which applies on Illinois waters, how many portable 5-B fire extinguishers must a vessel 26 to 40 feet long carry if it has no fixed (built-in) fire-extinguishing system in the machinery space?
choice_c: No portable extinguisher is required if there is no fixed system
explanation: Under 33 CFR 175.320, a vessel between 26 and 40 feet long without a qualifying fixed fire-extinguishing system in the machinery space must carry two portable 5-B fire extinguishers; a vessel with a qualifying fixed system may carry one fewer.
source_note: 33 CFR 175.320 (federal fire extinguisher carriage table, applicable to vessels on Illinois waters)

question: Under 33 CFR 175.320, how can a boater satisfy a requirement to carry two portable 5-B fire extinguishers by using a single higher-capacity extinguisher instead?
choice_a: By carrying one portable 20-B fire extinguisher, which may be substituted for two 5-B extinguishers
choice_b: By carrying one 5-B extinguisher and leaving the second required slot empty
choice_c: By carrying any household ABC extinguisher regardless of its rating
choice_d: Substitution of extinguisher types is not permitted under any circumstances
explanation: Federal fire extinguisher regulations allow one 20-B portable fire extinguisher to be substituted for two 5-B portable fire extinguishers, since it provides at least equivalent extinguishing capacity.

question: Under 33 CFR 175.320, when is a vessel less than 26 feet long, propelled only by outboard motor(s), exempt from having to carry a portable fire extinguisher?
choice_a: Whenever the operator holds a valid Illinois Boating Safety Certificate
choice_b: When the vessel's construction will not permit the entrapment of explosive or flammable gases or vapors
choice_c: Only if the vessel is registered specifically as a personal watercraft
choice_d: Never -- all outboard-powered vessels must carry a fire extinguisher regardless of size or construction
explanation: Federal law exempts an outboard-powered vessel under 26 feet from carrying a portable fire extinguisher only if its construction will not permit explosive or flammable gases or vapors to become trapped, such as having no closed compartments where fuel vapors could accumulate.

question: Portable marine fire extinguishers carried to meet federal requirements are rated '5-B' or '20-B.' What does the 'B' in this rating indicate?
choice_a: The extinguisher was manufactured in a specific production batch identified by the Coast Guard
choice_b: The extinguisher is effective only against electrical fires
choice_c: The extinguisher is designed for Class B fires -- fires fueled by flammable liquids such as gasoline and oil -- with the number reflecting its relative extinguishing capacity
choice_d: The extinguisher is rated for use only in fresh water, as opposed to salt water
explanation: The 'B' rating identifies an extinguisher as suited to Class B fires (flammable liquids like gasoline and oil) -- the type of fire most likely aboard a boat -- and the accompanying number reflects the extinguisher's relative firefighting capacity.

question: Under federal visual distress signal regulations (33 CFR 175.130), which device satisfies only the DAYTIME visual distress signal requirement, not the nighttime requirement?
choice_a: An electric distress light meeting 46 CFR 161.013
choice_b: A red hand-held flare meeting 46 CFR 160.021
choice_c: A red aerial pyrotechnic flare meeting 46 CFR 160.066
choice_d: An orange distress flag meeting 46 CFR 160.072
explanation: An orange distress flag meeting 46 CFR 160.072 satisfies only the day-use visual distress signal requirement; it is not effective at night and does not satisfy the nighttime requirement by itself.

question: Under federal visual distress signal regulations (33 CFR 175.130), which device satisfies ONLY the nighttime visual distress signal requirement?
choice_a: An electric distress light meeting 46 CFR 161.013
choice_b: An orange distress flag meeting 46 CFR 160.072
choice_d: Any ordinary flashlight carried on board
explanation: An electric distress light meeting 46 CFR 161.013 is approved to satisfy only the night-use visual distress signal requirement; an ordinary flashlight is not an approved distress signal device.

question: Under 33 CFR 175.130, if a boater chooses red hand-held flares to satisfy the day-and-night visual distress signal requirement, how many must be carried on board?
choice_d: There is no minimum quantity -- one is sufficient
explanation: Federal regulations require at least three red hand-held flares (or three parachute or aerial red flares) if that device is used to meet the day-and-night visual distress signal requirement.

question: Under 33 CFR 175.110, what visual distress signal requirement applies to a boat less than 16 feet long?
choice_a: It must carry both day and night signals at all times, identical to boats 16 feet and longer
choice_b: It is completely exempt from all visual distress signal requirements regardless of when it operates
choice_c: It must carry night-use signals only when operated between sunset and sunrise; no daytime signal is federally required
choice_d: It must carry day signals only and is never required to carry night signals
explanation: Under federal law, a boat less than 16 feet long is not required to carry daytime visual distress signals, but it must have night-use signals aboard if it operates between sunset and sunrise.

question: Under 33 CFR 183.610, which boats must be fitted with a powered ventilation (exhaust blower) system for compartments that are not open to the atmosphere?
choice_a: All vessels, regardless of engine or fuel type
choice_d: Boats with a permanently installed gasoline engine that has a cranking motor
explanation: Federal construction standards require boats with a permanently installed gasoline engine that has a cranking motor to have an exhaust blower system for compartments that aren't open to the atmosphere, since diesel fuel does not present the same explosive vapor hazard.

question: Federal regulation 33 CFR 183.610 requires boats with a powered ventilation system to post a warning label near the ignition switch. According to that label, what must a boater do before starting the engine?
choice_a: Operate the blower for 4 minutes and check the engine compartment bilge for gasoline vapors
choice_b: Open all portholes for at least 30 seconds
choice_c: Disconnect the battery for 4 minutes to release static charge
choice_d: Run the bilge pump continuously for 10 minutes
explanation: The federally required warning label reads: 'WARNING -- GASOLINE VAPORS CAN EXPLODE. BEFORE STARTING ENGINE OPERATE BLOWER FOR 4 MINUTES AND CHECK ENGINE COMPARTMENT BILGE FOR GASOLINE VAPORS.'

question: Under 33 CFR 183.610, where must the intake duct opening for a boat's powered ventilation system be located within the compartment it serves?
choice_a: At the very top of the compartment, near the overhead
choice_b: In the lower one-third of the compartment, above the normal level of accumulated bilge water
choice_c: Directly submerged in the bilge water at the bottom of the compartment
choice_d: Its location is not regulated as long as a blower is installed somewhere on board
explanation: Federal standards require the intake duct opening of a powered ventilation system to sit in the lower one-third of the compartment, positioned above the normal level of accumulated bilge water, so it draws heavier-than-air gasoline vapors out effectively.

question: Under 33 CFR 183.620, which of the following conditions requires a boat's compartment to be fitted with a natural ventilation system?
choice_a: The compartment is used only for dry storage of life jackets
choice_b: The compartment houses only the anchor and anchor line
choice_c: The compartment contains a permanently installed fuel tank that vents into the compartment
choice_d: The compartment contains only the vessel's freshwater tank
explanation: Federal construction standards require natural ventilation for compartments that contain a permanently installed fuel tank venting into the compartment, among other fuel- and engine-related conditions, because vented fuel vapors can otherwise accumulate and create an explosion hazard.
